body:
From the pre-release security review of the server's network interface
(2026-07-26). Post-1.8.1.

## Problem

NOT exploitable as written — verified. This is a latent hole held shut by an
accident, and it should be closed deliberately.

The invite token payload is colon-delimited (invites.py:36):

    f"{invite_id}:{list_id}:{email}:{expires_at}"

mint() explicitly rejects ':' in invited_email (invites.py:78, with a comment
naming decode_token as the reason) but does NOT reject ':' in list_id. And list
ids are arbitrary client-minted strings: _apply_list accepts any non-empty
string up to ID_MAX_LENGTH (128), with no charset restriction, and auto-grants
membership to the creator.

So the server can be made to HMAC-sign an attacker-shaped payload. Reproduced:

    list id created via /sync:
      'TARGETLIST:attacker@evil.com:99999999999999'
    resulting signed token plaintext:
      '<uuid>:TARGETLIST:attacker@evil.com:99999999999999:victim@example.com:1785713359034'

Redemption fails today: decode_token does split(":", 3), so the tail always
still contains the real email, and int(expires_at_str) raises -> 400
invalid_token. Confirmed by walking every case — with k colons injected into
list_id, the 4th field always retains the ':email:expires' suffix, so no k
produces a forgeable token.

The only thing separating this from "join any list whose id you can name" is
that int() cast. A refactor of decode_token (e.g. switching to rsplit for the
expiry, or reordering fields) silently turns it into arbitrary list-membership
theft, with no test that would catch it.

## Fix (defence in depth — do all three, they are each cheap)

1. mint(): reject ':' in list_id, mirroring the existing invited_email check,
   with the same reasoning in the comment.
2. redeem() (invites.py:110): take list_id from the DB invite row, not from the
   token. It already SELECTs the row for revoked/used_at — it just does not read
   list_id from it, and inserts the membership using the token's copy instead.
   The DB row is authoritative and unforgeable by construction.
3. Consider restricting client-minted list/item ids to a safe charset at
   _parse_row. Arbitrary 128-byte strings as primary keys is a broad surface —
   ':' is the one that bit here, but it is not obviously the only delimiter any
   future code will care about.

## Verification

Test that minting for a colon-bearing list id is rejected, and a test that
redeem joins the list named by the DB row even if a (hypothetically) mismatched
token is presented.
title: invites: colon in client-minted list_id reaches the signed token payload (latent delimiter injection)
